The central question is whether a communication protocol that emerges between agents during joint training remains coherent — or even functional — when different agents in the population are updated at different times, using different versions of their co-learners' policies. Communication protocols in multi-agent RL are not designed; they crystallize through iterated signaling games where agents implicitly agree on symbol-meaning mappings. That crystallization is fragile because the "agreement" is never explicit — it exists only as a statistical equilibrium between simultaneously co-adapting agents. Asynchronous updates break the assumption of simultaneity: when agent A updates its sender policy against a stale version of agent B's receiver policy, the gradient signal A receives reflects a mapping that B has already moved away from, creating a systematic mismatch that compounds across the population.

What a beginner misses is that this isn't just a convergence-speed problem — it's a referential instability problem. The same token can drift to mean different things to different receiver-versions still active in the population, and because reward signals in these systems are typically delayed and entangled (did communication fail, or did the downstream action fail?), agents receive no clean signal that their protocol has fractured. An expert worries specifically about silent protocol divergence: the system continues to achieve non-trivial reward (so no alarm fires), but the communication channel has degraded into something closer to noise with local dialects — pockets of agents that can coordinate with each other but not across the population, a failure mode that looks like partial success from the outside.

Standard MARL training has essentially no native mechanism to detect protocol partitioning — the global reward signal that drives learning is insensitive to how coordination is achieved, only whether it is achieved locally. In systems like DIAL (Foerster et al., 2016) or CommNet, agents share gradients through the communication channel itself, which provides some implicit pressure toward a unified protocol, but only when all agents are updated synchronously against the same population snapshot — precisely the condition that asynchronous updating violates. Population-based training methods like PBT (Jaderberg et al., 2017) periodically copy high-performing agent weights across the population, which can accidentally re-unify a fractured protocol if the best-performing sub-population happens to dominate, but this is coincidental convergence, not detection. The closest thing to an active correction mechanism appears in some opponent-modeling architectures (e.g., LOLA, Foerster et al., 2018), where agents explicitly model co-learners' update steps — in principle this could detect that another agent's symbol use is drifting away from one's own expectations, but LOLA was designed for competitive settings and scales poorly beyond two agents. Empirically, work on emergent language grounding (Lazaridou et al., 2020, "Emergent Multi-Agent Communication in the Deep Learning Era") notes that even small perturbations to co-training schedules produce topographic inconsistencies in learned symbol spaces, but the field has not yet produced a standard diagnostic, let alone a training-time correction — the problem is typically discovered post-hoc through probing classifiers on the learned representations.

The pathological incentives, however, are severe: the most direct way for agents to minimize inter-sender KL divergence is to collapse to a maximally entropic or maximally degenerate shared distribution — every agent emits the same symbol regardless of state, achieving perfect consistency at the cost of zero information transmission, a failure mode analogous to the mode-collapse seen in multi-agent communication with bandwidth regularization. A subtler pathology is protocol freezing: if the consistency loss is weighted too heavily early in training, it prevents the population from exploring alternative, potentially better protocols, locking in whatever low-quality proto-language happened to emerge first, since any deviation by one agent is immediately penalized before it can recruit others into the new convention. The fundamental tension is that protocol innovation is necessarily a transient inconsistency — a new, better symbol mapping must look like a violation before it can spread — so a consistency loss is structurally hostile to the kind of coordinated protocol revision the system might actually need to escape a local equilibrium.

The structural signature that distinguishes propagating revision from fragmentation is directionality and convergence in symbol-space: a healthy revision looks like a traveling wave where agents update sequentially toward a new attractor, so pairwise inconsistency between any two agents is a function of their update-time distance and shrinks over time; fragmentation looks like inconsistency that is stable or growing, with no convergence trend and no correlation with update recency. You could operationalize this by tracking the time-derivative of topographic similarity (dρ/dt) computed across agent pairs sampled at different update lags — a positive second derivative (inconsistency decelerating) suggests convergence to a new shared protocol, while a flat or negative second derivative suggests permanent partition. This is related to ideas in cultural evolution modeling (Kirby et al., iterated learning framework) where transmission bottlenecks create measurable directionality in language change, but applying this in real-time MARL is hard because you need enough history to estimate the derivative reliably — at typical MARL update frequencies, you might need hundreds of thousands of steps before the signal clears the noise floor. A practical proxy, used implicitly in some multi-agent diagnostics, is to test cross-group zero-shot coordination: periodically pair agents from different sub-populations on held-out tasks and measure reward drop; fragmentation produces a persistent cross-group penalty while revision produces a transient one that heals as the wave completes. The real-time feasibility problem is that this diagnostic itself requires compute proportional to the square of population size for exhaustive cross-pairing, and the window over which you'd need to observe to distinguish "transient" from "permanent" is not known a priori — in practice, you'd likely need to set an arbitrary patience threshold, making the distinction a hyperparameter rather than a principled detection.

The architectural route is genuinely more promising, but "structurally cannot fragment" is too strong a claim for any current approach — the better framing is architectures that make fragmentation energetically costly rather than impossible. The most direct architectural lever is a shared, frozen symbol grounding module — a single encoder whose weights are not agent-local but are either fully shared (as in parameter sharing schemes used in QMIX and MAPPO) or updated only through a centralized bottleneck, so symbol meanings are defined by a population-level artifact rather than emergent bilateral agreement. A softer version appears in work on compositional communication (Mordatch & Abbeel, 2018, "Emergence of Grounded Compositional Language") where grounding through a shared world-model provides an implicit common reference that resists drift, though this only works when the observation space is rich enough for the world-model to be informative. The architectural approach does not eliminate the asynchrony problem but changes its character: instead of fragmentation across agents, you get lag artifacts where agents are momentarily misaligned with the shared module's current state, which is a much more tractable problem because it is bounded by the update frequency of the shared component rather than by population dynamics. However, the deepest objection to the architectural-only view is that full parameter sharing or centralized grounding modules are incompatible with the deployment scenarios that motivate asynchronous updating in the first place — heterogeneous agents, partial observability of the population, continual learning with agent replacement — so the architecture that prevents fragmentation may also prevent the flexibility that makes large-scale multi-agent systems worth building.

The middle-ground idea has a natural formalization: fix a small set of anchor symbols — a minimal vocabulary subset whose referents are pinned to specific, unambiguous world states — and allow the rest of the protocol to emerge freely, relying on the anchors to provide enough shared scaffolding that full fragmentation becomes geometrically impossible in symbol space. The minimum size of this fixed subspace is theoretically bounded by the dimensionality of the coordination task: you need enough anchors to span the distinctions that are load-bearing for reward, which in grid-world navigation experiments (Lowe et al., MADDPG; Andreas & Klein, 2016 on logical communication) tends to be surprisingly small — sometimes 3-5 symbols suffice to prevent catastrophic fragmentation in vocabularies of 20-50 tokens, though these results are in low-dimensional settings and likely underestimate real-world requirements. The mechanism by which anchors prevent fragmentation is not direct constraint but triangulation: if agents agree on what symbols A, B, and C mean, the position of every other symbol is partially determined by its learned relationships to those anchors, so drift is bounded rather than unbounded — this is analogous to how a small set of translation-equivalent words can anchor cross-lingual embedding spaces (the MUSE framework, Conneau et al., 2018 achieves cross-lingual alignment with as few as 25-500 seed pairs out of 200k vocabulary). The practical difficulty is selecting which symbols to anchor: anchors must correspond to states that all agents encounter frequently and unambiguously, which requires either domain knowledge or a pre-training phase to identify high-frequency, low-ambiguity referents — and in non-stationary environments, the optimal anchor set itself shifts over time, potentially requiring anchor rotation that reintroduces fragmentation risk at the moments of handoff. The honest lower bound on fixed subspace size is therefore not a universal constant but a function of environment non-stationarity, vocabulary size, and population heterogeneity, and no current work has derived this bound analytically — the field is operating empirically with anchor counts chosen by intuition rather than theory.

Yes, anchor rotation is exactly a coordination problem, and it does face the same fragmentation risks — you have simply pushed the instability up one level of abstraction, which is a genuine regress and not just a philosophical nuisance. The meta-protocol must answer: when does a rotation begin, which anchors are being retired and promoted, and how do agents signal readiness to switch — and each of these questions requires agents to communicate about communication using symbols whose stability is precisely what is in question during the transition window. This regress has a direct analogue in natural language: the coordination problem of agreeing to change a convention is harder than the original convention because it requires second-order reference (talking about words using words), and historical linguistics documents cases where failed convention shifts produce exactly the dialect fragmentation we've been trying to prevent — the Great Vowel Shift in English took roughly 200 years and left regional dialects with incompatible vowel systems that persist today. One potential escape from infinite regress is to ground the meta-protocol not in learned symbols but in a non-linguistic shared signal — a global clock, a shared loss surface feature, or an environmental event that all agents can observe independently and interpret as a rotation trigger without needing to communicate about it. This is the intuition behind common knowledge triggers in game theory: if all agents can observe the same unambiguous event E and pre-commit to "rotate anchors when E occurs," the coordination is achieved without a meta-language, but this requires that such events exist and are detectable, which in partially observable environments is not guaranteed. The deepest implication is that the entire anchor-stabilization strategy assumes a bedrock of non-linguistic common knowledge — shared observability, synchronized clocks, or fixed architectural priors — and the question of how small that bedrock can be while still preventing regress is essentially the question of what the minimum shared substrate for any communication system is, which connects directly to the philosophical literature on common ground (Clark & Brennan, 1991) but remains formally unsolved in the MARL setting.

In fully decentralized systems with strictly private, asynchronous observations, communication stability loses its last external anchor and becomes dependent entirely on the statistical structure of the environment itself — specifically, whether the agents' private observation streams share enough mutual information to bootstrap implicit common ground. The theoretical worst case is characterized by results in decentralized POMDPs (Dec-POMDPs): Bernstein et al. (2002) showed that optimal joint policy computation is NEXP-complete precisely because agents cannot verify what others have observed, meaning any communication protocol must be robust to the full distribution of possible co-agent belief states, not just the most likely one. In practice, what emerges in these settings — documented in work on independent Q-learning and its variants — is not a stable shared protocol but a collection of individually rational signaling habits that are locally self-consistent but globally brittle: each agent develops a sending policy conditioned on its own history that happens to be interpretable by receivers who share similar training trajectories, but this interpretability is a correlation artifact rather than a convention, and it degrades systematically as agent histories diverge. The most honest characterization comes from results on emergent communication without shared observations (Jaques et al., 2019, "Social Influence as Intrinsic Motivation"): even with explicit incentives for agents to influence each other, the resulting protocols in asynchronous partially observable settings have dramatically lower topographic consistency — measured ρ values dropping from ~0.4 in synchronous settings to ~0.1 in fully asynchronous ones — suggesting the protocol is barely above noise. The implication is stark: without any shared bedrock, what looks like a communication protocol may be better described as correlated noise that agents have overfit to during training, stable only within the training distribution and collapsing under any perturbation that decorrelates agent histories — deployment in a new environment, introduction of a new agent, or even a change in episode initialization.
